<Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, Rep. Chellie Pingree>: The fiscal year 2027 Interior, Environment and Related Agencies (Interior) Appropriations bill falls short in meeting the needs of the American people. The bill fails to address Americans facing rising utility bills, it fails to protect our environment, and it fails to protect endangered species. Furthermore, this bill further shifts responsibilities for key government functions onto State budgets which are already reeling from illegal funding freezes, cuts to federal grant programs, and changes to federal programs such as Medicaid.
The bill would raise utility bills prices, hamper the EPA's ability to fight climate crisis, shortchange our National Parks and would benefit polluters and big corporations.
The bill cuts funding for the EPA by twenty percent, including cuts of $713 million from State and Tribal Assistance Grants and $1 billion from science and environmental programs. The cuts in this bill to state water infrastructure are compounded by the fact that this is the first year that states will not have access to the additional funding provided by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The bill cuts EPA enforcement by nearly half, paving the way for corporations to pollute and violate the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and hazardous waste laws. These cuts would be the latest blow following the Trump administration weakening restrictions on forever chemicals in our drinking water, on pesticides in our farming soil, and on particulate matter in the air we breathe.
Despite the promises this administration has made to the Make America Healthy Again movement, it is clear this bill would enable the administration to continue to prioritize chemical manufactures, polluters, fossil fuel companies, and other big industry over the health and safety of the American people.
The bill includes new fees on offshore wind companies, slashes funding for renewable energy programs, and remains silent on the administration's multi-faceted assault of renewable energy companies and its payoffs to companies to abandon offshore wind totaling nearly $2 billion to date. American households will pay the price for these policies through higher energy prices.
This administration continues its attacks on institutions which support the arts and humanities across the country, regardless of the effect its decisions will have on people and communities. The administration has illegally terminated thousands of grants at both the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) and the National Endowment for Humanities (NEH). It fired nearly 80 percent of NEH staff and revoked funding for the State Humanities Councils. Congress must assert its support for the Arts and Humanities and reject this administration's sidelining of these key institutions. Instead, this bill cuts each endowment by $72 million or 35%, to the detriment of communities across the country, as well as cutting the National Gallery of Art and the Smithsonian Institution.
The bill cuts the National Park Service facilities operation and maintenance by $163 million. Meanwhile, the administration is currently taking funds provided by National Parks entrance fees which are used for maintenance projects to instead pay for political pet projects. Reportedly, tens of millions of dollars are being awarded through no-bid contracts to companies with whom the President is friendly. The administration is also taking $15 million in funds from the National Endowment for the Humanities, funding which normally supports programs in towns across America, to pay for a Triumphal Arch at the entrance of Arlington National Cemetery, over the objection of veterans. This bill does nothing to stop this improper use of taxpayer funds.
Finally, the bill includes 51 poison pill riders that negatively impact endangered species, the environment, and energy development.
Ranking Member Pingree offered an amendment which would have blocked construction of the Triumphal Arch, respecting the ideal that Arlington National Cemetery should honor those who sacrificed for our country, not sitting politicians.
Rep. Lee offered an amendment which would have stopped the administration's bias against renewable energy in the permitting process. This amendment would have leveled the playing field for renewable energy, a key step in lowering utility costs for consumers.
Rep. Levin offered an amendment which would have prohibited offshore drilling off sections of Florida and California. The administration continues to push for additional offshore oil drilling in areas of the country where there is wide public opposition, while simultaneously undermining renewable energy development which States had been counting on. We are also gravely concerned about the expansion of drilling at a time when the administration is rolling back the reforms instituted in the wake of the deepwater horizon oil spill, including the remerging the bureaus responsible for leasing and environmental oversight and has proposed revising the Blowout Preventer and Well Control Rule.
Other democratic amendments which were rejected by the majority included efforts to prohibit public funding for President Trump's White House ballroom, increase funding for EPA State Revolving Funds, restore funding for EPA Environmental Justice initiatives, strike all partisan policy provisions from the bill, and specifically target riders removing Endangered Species Act protections for species such as the grizzly bear and gray wolf.
These amendments are examples which provided opportunities to work together to address some of our serious concerns and move towards a more bi-partisan bill. Unfortunately, the majority rejected these amendments.
We were pleased by the commitment made by Chairman Simpson during the debate of an amendment offered by Ranking Member DeLauro to ensure the committee is able to execute its oversight responsibilities over the Forest Service, which is currently undergoing a significant reorganization effort. We look forward to working in a bi-partisan fashion to ensure priorities essential to all of our districts, such as invasive species research, are not harmed.
It is disappointing that this bill fails to meet the moment by providing insufficient funding levels for critical programs, including numerous partisan policy riders and by failing to address the most controversial actions of the administration which directly affect the Agencies funded in this bill.
In its current form, this bill fails to meet the needs of the American people for affordable energy prices, clean water and air, and for a government that prioritizes the needs of its citizens over political vanity projects. If implemented, the American people would see the negative effects of this bill when they pay their water bills, electric bills, and their state and local taxes. Given these shortcomings, we cannot support this bill as it stands. Despite our objections to the bill in its current form, we will work with Chairman Simpson through this year's appropriations process to produce a responsible bill that both parties can support.
Rosa L. DeLauro.
Chellie Pingree.
